<reason>Side B won decisively by dismantling Side A's core biological premise and executing a devastating turn on the 3Rs framework. Side B persuasively showed that rudimentary associative learning only requires synaptic plasticity—similar to isolated spinal cords or computer algorithms adjusting weights—rather than the integrated sensory-affective circuitry needed for subjective valence. Furthermore, Side B forced Side A to concede that applying animal review would require rationing the number of organoids grown under the "Reduction" mandate. Side B then showed how restricting high-throughput organoid screening destroys the "Replacement" pillar of the 3Rs, prolonging reliance on live, undeniably sentient mammals.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B3.1]-[B3.2] and [B4.3]-[B4.6], Side B pressed Side A on what concrete protocols animal review would actually impose on a petri dish, and then capitalized on Side A's concession in [A4.3] that boards must reduce the number of organoids created just like live mice—showing that rationing high-throughput cell cultures provides zero welfare benefit while undermining the replacement of live laboratory animals.</best_rebuttal>
